title: Classes, Objects and Modules
subtitle: Classes, Objects and Modules: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on classes, objects and modules, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Classes, Objects and Modules: foundations and mental model

Classes, Objects and Modules is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Types group related state and behavior. Initialize valid values, protect invariants, and use inheritance or composition only when it improves the model. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A tracker illustrates how collection methods can keep business logic readable. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Classes, Objects and Modules: initialize sets instance state and attr_reader exposes read access
blocks.code:
class Learner
  attr_reader :name, :xp
  def initialize(name, xp)
    @name, @xp = name, xp
  end
end
puts Learner.new("Ama", 120).name
blocks.output: initialize sets instance state and attr_reader exposes read access.

blocks.question: A learner record contains name and XP. What is the main benefit of grouping them in one model?
options: Related state stays together and can be validated through a clear interface
The model automatically saves itself to Firebase
Every field becomes safe from modification automatically
All records must share the same XP value
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Related state stays together and can be validated through a clear interface. A model expresses a domain entity, but persistence and encapsulation still require deliberate implementation.
blocks.reasoning: A model expresses a domain entity, but persistence and encapsulation still require deliberate implementation. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Classes, Objects and Modules: A module groups reusable functionality without creating an instance
blocks.code:
module ProgressRules
  def self.percent(done, total)
    total.positive? ? done.to_f / total * 100 : 0
  end
end
blocks.output: A module groups reusable functionality without creating an instance.

blocks.question: Several types must provide `report()`, but their internal data differs. Which abstraction is suitable?
options: Copy the same method into unrelated caller code
Use one global variable for all records
Store source code in the report field
An interface or protocol describing the required behavior
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: An interface or protocol describing the required behavior. An interface or protocol defines a contract without requiring identical internal representations.
blocks.reasoning: An interface or protocol defines a contract without requiring identical internal representations. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Classes, Objects and Modules: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Types group related state and behavior. Initialize valid values, protect invariants, and use inheritance or composition only when it improves the model. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A tracker illustrates how collection methods can keep business logic readable. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Classes, Objects and Modules: A method can expose behavior using the instance state
blocks.code:
class Lesson
  def label
    "Lesson: #{title}"
  end
  attr_reader :title
  def initialize(title) = @title = title
end
blocks.output: A method can expose behavior using the instance state.

blocks.question: A course-progress object must never have a negative total. Where should that rule be protected?
options: Only when the object is printed
By assuming all call sites follow a comment
At the model or validation boundary that creates and updates the object
Only in the page heading
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: At the model or validation boundary that creates and updates the object. Domain invariants should be enforced where data enters or changes, not only at display time.
blocks.reasoning: Domain invariants should be enforced where data enters or changes, not only at display time. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Classes, Objects and Modules: Struct is a concise way to create a simple data object
blocks.code:
Course = Struct.new(:name, :lesson_count, keyword_init: true)
puts Course.new(name: "Ruby", lesson_count: 10)
blocks.output: Struct is a concise way to create a simple data object.

blocks.question: A type has only two fields and no behavior or identity requirements. What design principle applies?
options: Make all members globally mutable
Prefer the simplest data structure that clearly represents the value
Use inheritance by default
Create an abstract hierarchy for every field
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Prefer the simplest data structure that clearly represents the value. Classes, structs, and records should match actual domain needs rather than add ceremony.
blocks.reasoning: Classes, structs, and records should match actual domain needs rather than add ceremony. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Classes, Objects and Modules: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Types group related state and behavior. Initialize valid values, protect invariants, and use inheritance or composition only when it improves the model. For the Code Academy dashboard, A tracker illustrates how collection methods can keep business logic readable. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses classes, objects and modules. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A subclass overrides a method with an incompatible meaning. What is the key design risk?
options: The subtype may violate the contract expected by callers
The compiler must automatically rewrite all callers
The program gains database persistence
Object fields become inaccessible in every language
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: The subtype may violate the contract expected by callers. Subtyping is safe only when the subtype respects the behavioral expectations of its base contract.
blocks.reasoning: Subtyping is safe only when the subtype respects the behavioral expectations of its base contract. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Types group related state and behavior. Initialize valid values, protect invariants, and use inheritance or composition only when it improves the model. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
